26  III.  DISCUSSION                                                      
27       As further explained below, the Court ultimately agrees with two of the points raised 
1  sanctions.  Specifically,  Defendants  permissibly  withheld  documents  from  the  initial 
2  versions of the ARs as deliberative, but later admitted they had not reviewed between six 
3  and eight thousand of those documents before withholding them as deliberative—though 
4  BLM’s counsel also represented at the Hearing she was aware of no authority requiring 
5  BLM to review each document before withholding it. But nonetheless, and as RSIC points 
6  out, how could BLM’s counsel have known that those documents were deliberative if they 
7  had not yet reviewed them? BLM’s counsel essentially conceded at the Hearing that she 
8  could not.                                                            
9       Moreover, the affidavits that accompanied the versions of the ARs lodged with the 
10  Court arguably contain incorrect statements because of the way Defendants produced 
11  several versions of the ARs in this case. The Court uses the phrase arguably because Mr. 
12  Loda’s statements included caveats such as ‘based on my knowledge and information.’ 
13  But considering these two points together, the Court agrees that RSIC has highlighted a 
14  defective process in its Motion. And even BLM’s counsel admitted that there were some 
15  ‘speed bumps’ in the process leading to full production of the ARs here.  That said, 
16  Defendants and their counsel’s actions do not appear to have been taken intentionally in 
17  bad faith, nor were they reckless coupled with some other factor such as an intent to 
18  harass—and RSIC does not even really argue they were. Thus, sanctions under 28 U.S.C. 
19  § 1927 or the Court’s inherent powers are unavailable to RSIC here. Moreover, the Court 
20  agrees with Defendants that sanctions are unavailable under Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(b) in this 
21  case, without holding that Rule 37(b) sanctions are never available in any case including 
22  an APA claim. And in any event, any prejudice to the other parties due to Defendants’ 
23  counsel’s conduct in producing the ARs was not so great to warrant the severe sanctions 
24  RSIC seeks in its Motion—were those sanctions even available.         
25       To start, there was nothing impermissible or nefarious about Defendants’ decision 
26  to withhold deliberative documents from the first versions of the ARs that they produced. 
27  As Defendants argue, their position was supported by caselaw from the D.C. Circuit Court 
1  Moreover, that same body of caselaw supported Defendants’ decision not to log any 
2  omitted documents in a privilege log, because that line of caselaw holds that deliberative 
3  documents are simply not part of the administrative record. (Id. at 10-11.) In addition, 
4  Defendants timely produced the initial versions of the ARs. (ECF Nos. 94 at 3, 113 at 2.) 
5  Thus, the Court rejects RSIC’s arguments to the extent based on the initial production of 
6  the ARs.                                                              
7       However, Defendants do not have a persuasive response to RSIC’s valid point that 
8  Defendants excluded some six or eight thousand documents from the initial version of the 
9  ARs as deliberative without first reviewing them. (ECF Nos. 173 at 2, 200-2 (asking for 
10  more time to review six to eight thousand documents not previously included in the ARs); 
11  see also ECF Nos. 200 at 9-10 (noting this issue), 218 (declining to discuss in detail the 
12  six to eight thousand documents they had to review before producing the revised ARs), 
13  221 at 8-10 (again pointing out this issue).) Defendants should have reviewed these 
14  documents  instead  of  relying  on  their  designation  as  deliberative  based  on  the 
15  contemporaneous determinations of agency employees before withholding them from the 
16  ARs as deliberative.7 Indeed, this issue provides another reason supporting the Court’s 
17  decision to follow the District of Montana’s approach in Ksanka Kupaqa Xa’lcin v. United 
18  States Fish & Wildlife Serv., Case No. CV 19-20-M-DWM, 2020 WL 4193110 (D. Mont. 
19  Mar. 9, 2020) and require Defendants to include a privilege log with its revised ARs. (ECF 
20  No. 155 at 4-6.) If Defendants were required to provide a privilege log from the outset, 
21  they would have had to review all relevant documents before producing the first versions 
22  of the ARs to decide what to include in the privilege log. Thus, they could not have 
23  overlooked six to eight thousand documents so easily. And this issue further illustrates the

4       But none of the argument or evidence presented by RSIC in its Motion or at the 
5  Hearing—and discussed supra—tends to evidence intentional conduct, much less bad 
6  faith. Indeed, RSIC ultimately concedes as much in its reply brief, writing, “RSIC may be 
7  forgiven for concluding that at some point, ‘inadvertence’ gives way to ‘recklessness,’ and 
8  ‘recklessness’ forms the basis for a conclusion of ‘intentionality[,]’” and then declining to 
9  specify precisely which sanction is appropriate here. (ECF No. 221 at 14.) And because 
10  the Court does not find that the errors described above evidence bad faith, the Court also 
11  finds that any sanction under either Section 1927 or the Court’s inherent powers would be 
12  inappropriate. Indeed, even recklessness is insufficient to sanction an attorney under the 
13  Court’s inherent powers, though “an award of attorney’s fees is justified when reckless 
14  conduct is ‘combined with an additional factor such as frivolousness, harassment, or an 
15  improper purpose.’” Rodriguez v. United States, 542 F.3d 704, 709 (9th Cir. 2008) (citation 
16  omitted). Similarly, the Court may find bad faith under Section 1927 either when subjective 
17  bad faith is present or when “‘an attorney knowingly or recklessly raises a frivolous 
18  argument or argues a meritorious claim for the purpose of harassing an opponent.’” 
19  Blixseth v. Yellowstone Mountain Club, LLC, 796 F.3d 1004, 1007 (9th Cir. 2015). None 
20  of this describes Defendants’ counsels’ conduct here.                 
21       And while the Court will not foreclose the possibility of ever awarding Rule 37(b) 
22  sanctions in a case that involves an APA claim,9 the Court finds that it would be improper

4  Thus, none of the specifically-mentioned examples in Rule 37(b)(2)(A) apply. And the 
5  Court does not find that its December 2021 Order is “an order to provide or permit

15  traditional discovery has occurred in this case, so the traditional remedies for discovery 
16  violations do not apply.

10  unpersuasive because, for example, the Court denied that motion in part because the 
11  proposed amended complaint attempted to assert claims on behalf of an unclear number 
12  of additional tribes who were not RSIC. (ECF No. 167 at 6-8.) That finding would not have

14       Second, RSIC has not made a persuasive showing that its requested sanctions are 
15  commensurate to the scale of Defendants’ violations. Most notably, RSIC seeks case-
16  dispositive sanctions right as the merits briefing process is getting underway. (ECF No. 
17  200  at  22-25.)  RSIC  proffers  no  applicable  law  supporting  its  request  for  a  default 
18  judgment vacating the ROD and remanding to BLM. And the Court is aware of no such 
19  authority. It would be an abuse of the Court’s discretion to allow RSIC’s attempted end-
20  run around the merits briefing process because RSIC caught Defendants in two ‘gotchas.’ 
21  While it is now clear that the Court will be unable to resolve this case on any particular 
22  timetable, it wishes to resolve this case on the merits. As even RSIC concedes, public 
23  policy favors it. (Id. at 24 (quoting Adriana Intern. Corp. v. Thoerenm, 913 F.2d 1406, 1412 
24  (9th Cir. 1990)).)                                                    
25  IV.  CONCLUSION                                                       
26       The Court notes that the parties made several arguments and cited to several cases 
27  not discussed above. The Court has reviewed these arguments and cases and determines 
1  || that they do not warrant discussion as they do not affect the outcome of the Motion before 
2 || the Court. 
3          It is therefore ordered that RSIC’s motion for sanctions (ECF No. 200) is denied.

26  III.  DISCUSSION                                                      
27       As further explained below, the Court ultimately agrees with two of the points raised 
1  sanctions.  Specifically,  Defendants  permissibly  withheld  documents  from  the  initial 
2  versions of the ARs as deliberative, but later admitted they had not reviewed between six 
3  and eight thousand of those documents before withholding them as deliberative—though 
4  BLM’s counsel also represented at the Hearing she was aware of no authority requiring 
5  BLM to review each document before withholding it. But nonetheless, and as RSIC points 
6  out, how could BLM’s counsel have known that those documents were deliberative if they 
7  had not yet reviewed them? BLM’s counsel essentially conceded at the Hearing that she 
8  could not.                                                            
9       Moreover, the affidavits that accompanied the versions of the ARs lodged with the 
10  Court arguably contain incorrect statements because of the way Defendants produced 
11  several versions of the ARs in this case. The Court uses the phrase arguably because Mr. 
12  Loda’s statements included caveats such as ‘based on my knowledge and information.’ 
13  But considering these two points together, the Court agrees that RSIC has highlighted a 
14  defective process in its Motion. And even BLM’s counsel admitted that there were some 
15  ‘speed bumps’ in the process leading to full production of the ARs here.  That said, 
16  Defendants and their counsel’s actions do not appear to have been taken intentionally in 
17  bad faith, nor were they reckless coupled with some other factor such as an intent to 
18  harass—and RSIC does not even really argue they were. Thus, sanctions under 28 U.S.C. 
19  § 1927 or the Court’s inherent powers are unavailable to RSIC here. Moreover, the Court 
20  agrees with Defendants that sanctions are unavailable under Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(b) in this 
21  case, without holding that Rule 37(b) sanctions are never available in any case including 
22  an APA claim. And in any event, any prejudice to the other parties due to Defendants’ 
23  counsel’s conduct in producing the ARs was not so great to warrant the severe sanctions 
24  RSIC seeks in its Motion—were those sanctions even available.         
25       To start, there was nothing impermissible or nefarious about Defendants’ decision 
26  to withhold deliberative documents from the first versions of the ARs that they produced. 
27  As Defendants argue, their position was supported by caselaw from the D.C. Circuit Court
